e.t: This word refers to byssus, a fine white linen fabric. As a noun, it names a material rather than an action, person, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 4:21. The precise way the material functions in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic meaning is the fabric itself: linen distinguished by its fineness and white appearance.

Abou is a proper name, also given as “Avu.” It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs once, in 2 Kings 18:2. The available information establishes its naming function and its two supplied renderings, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whom or what the name identifies in that passage.

This word means “brotherhood”: a bond or community understood in terms of brothers. It functions as a noun, naming that shared relationship rather than describing an individual person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs seven times, all in deuterocanonical books, especially 4 Maccabees and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains brotherhood or a relationship of shared kinship.

This word means “discomfort.” It refers to a state of discomfort or a quality marked by discomfort. As a noun, it names that condition; as an adjective, it describes something characterized by it. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, four in 4 Maccabees and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on context.

This word means “salt,” the familiar mineral substance used in food and other ordinary settings. It is a noun, naming the substance rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times, including passages from Genesis, Leviticus, Numbers, Joshua, Chronicles, Job, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical meaning remains salt.

This noun means “abominable wickedness”—conduct marked by extreme moral evil and regarded as deeply detestable. It names wickedness not merely as wrongdoing, but as something especially loathsome. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a strong description of abhorrent wickedness.

Anathōth is a proper name rendered “Anathoth.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general term describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 14 times across 14 verses, including passages in Joshua, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Jeremiah. Its repeated use identifies the same named referent wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular significance in each passage.

Anani is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It does not function as a general word describing an idea, action, or quality; it identifies particular individuals named Anani. The name occurs 10 times in 10 Old Testament verses, appearing in Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Because it is a personal name, its specific referent must be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the name itself. It is rendered “Anani” in the available English support.

This word means “baldness on the forehead,” describing a bare or hairless area at the front of the head. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament, where it occurs three times in two verses of Leviticus 13, all within the discussion recorded in that chapter. The term identifies a visible physical condition rather than expressing an action or feeling. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the distinctions made there.

This noun refers to a people-pleaser—someone characterized by seeking to satisfy or win the approval of other people. It names a person rather than an action, and its basic meaning focuses on pleasing humans. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 52:6; the surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s specific force in that passage cannot be described further. Its central idea remains a person oriented toward gaining human approval.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “rebuke” or “blame”: it describes speaking against someone to point out fault or hold that person responsible. Its basic force is corrective or accusing rather than merely describing a mistake. In the Greek rendering of Job, it occurs once, at Job 33:27, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding words. The related English rendering is “blame,” which fits the word’s central idea of assigning fault.

This verb means to show something forth or display it openly. It describes making something evident by presenting or declaring it, rather than keeping it concealed. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, appearing in Job and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being brought forward and the surrounding sentence.

Asimath is a proper name rendered as “Asimath.” It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but as a particular name preserved in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 2 Kings 17:30. Without the verse text and surrounding context, the available information identifies the name and its location but does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or other named entity.

This adjective describes something that is out of place or impertinent—unfitting, improper, or unsuitable in the situation. It can characterize conduct, words, or a condition that does not belong or is not acceptable. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, the word occurs eight times, chiefly in Job. Its central idea remains the same: something is wrong because it is out of order, inappropriate, or offensive rather than fitting the circumstances.

This noun refers to immunity—being released from an obligation—or to remission of tribute, meaning that a payment or tax is canceled or no longer required. It describes an official exemption rather than a personal feeling or private decision. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is release from tribute or another imposed obligation.

This word means “up to” or “until,” marking the point where an action, movement, or period reaches its limit. It is a preposition that connects something with that endpoint. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: twice in the Old Testament and twice in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains the same whether it points to a place, a boundary, or a time. The surrounding words determine exactly what endpoint it identifies.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Badekar” or “Vathekar.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 9:25. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise role in that passage cannot be explained further here. The name itself should therefore be understood as a personal designation, with the spelling “Badekar” or “Vathekar” representing the same source-word identity.

Baithakad, also rendered Vethakath, is a proper name for a place named in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a description of a person, action, or quality, but a geographic name preserved as a place-name. This LXX form occurs twice, both in 2 Kings, at 2 Kings 10:12 and 10:14. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse context.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to “cast” or “throw”—to send or move something through the air or place it somewhere by a deliberate action. It can describe the ordinary act of throwing, casting lots, or putting something where it belongs, with the surrounding sentence determining the precise use. The word occurs 50 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, so it expresses a recurring action rather than a rare technical term. Its listed uses include Judges 8:25 and 1 Chronicles 26:14.

This word means “frog,” the name of the amphibious animal. It is a noun used for one frog or for frogs as a group, depending on the sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 15 times, chiefly in Exodus, where frogs are repeatedly mentioned, with additional occurrences in Psalms and Wisdom. Its basic meaning remains straightforward and concrete: it identifies the creature itself rather than expressing an abstract quality or action.

The word refers to “Bēth,” a noun used as a name or designation. Its lexical meaning is therefore not an action, quality, or relationship, but the identifying term itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs one time, in Psalm 118:9. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding biblical wording, but its basic lexical sense remains the named term “Bēth.”

This word means “meal” or “eating,” referring to food or the act of taking food. It is a noun used for nourishment in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. The word appears 37 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages from Genesis, Leviticus, Psalms, Jeremiah, and Lamentations. Its basic sense remains focused on food consumed or the practice of eating, while the surrounding verse determines the precise emphasis. It is first found in Genesis 1:29 and last found in Wisdom 4:5.

Gesouri, also called Yesuri, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person or people by name, but the available information does not establish which one from the name alone. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 12:5. Its precise referent must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “resolve”: a settled decision, determination, or purpose. As a noun, it refers to what someone has firmly decided or intends to carry out. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 30 times, showing a repeated use for decisive purpose rather than a passing thought or uncertain opinion. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a firm determination or settled decision.

This verb means to “bundle up” or “tether”—to tie things together or fasten them so they are held in place. It can describe physically binding or securing something, rather than merely touching or gathering it. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented here, including uses across Genesis, Judges, 1 Samuel, Job, Psalms, Amos, and 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being tied and the surrounding sentence.

It is a verb meaning to “speak plainly” or “declare”—to express something openly and clearly rather than leave it uncertain. The word focuses on making a statement known in direct speech. Its precise force in Susanna 1:60 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, since the verse text is not included here. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once.

This Greek verb means “cast”: to throw or send something away from oneself. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears two times, once in Job and once in Isaiah, with the same English rendering, “cast.” Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the basic word consistently expresses the act of casting or throwing.

This adjective describes someone or something that is “thirsty”—experiencing or expressing a desire for drink. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Proverbs 9:12. The word gives a physical description, while the precise force of that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central meaning remains straightforward: it identifies thirst or a thirsting condition rather than naming a person, place, or action.

This word means “gratuitously” or “freely”: something is given, received, or done without requiring payment or compensation. It describes an action or benefit offered without charge, rather than something earned through a stated price. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 26 times across 26 verses, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Psalms, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what the surrounding sentence says is being given or done freely.

“Peaceably” means in a peaceful, non-hostile manner. As an adverb, it describes how someone acts, speaks, approaches, or settles something—not a person or object itself. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) material represented here, this word appears four times, all in 1–2 Maccabees. Its basic force is conduct marked by peace rather than conflict. The surrounding verse determines what action is being described.

“Ecclesiastes” is a proper name used in the Greek Septuagint text of the book of Ecclesiastes. It serves as a designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The word occurs seven times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, all within Ecclesiastes, from 1:1 through 12:10. Its precise role in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function is to identify a named figure or speaker.

This Greek LXX verb means to “drink out,” describing the action of consuming a drink completely or drinking from it. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Job, Isaiah, Zechariah, and Bel and the Dragon. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being consumed and the surrounding sentence.

This noun means an “olive-tree” or an “olive,” referring to the tree itself or its fruit. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Micah. Its basic meaning remains consistent: it identifies the familiar olive tree or what that tree produces. The surrounding verse determines whether the reference points more naturally to the plant or to the olive fruit, but the word itself carries this straightforward meaning.

This Greek LXX verb expresses the action of “frequent” or “measure by.” It can describe either repeated association with a place or person, or using something as a standard of measurement, depending on the sentence. The word appears seven times in the LXX corpus, including passages in Joshua, 1 Maccabees, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This adjective means “glorious.” It describes a person, thing, or condition characterized by glory and distinction. In ordinary Bible language, it points to what is honored, splendid, or held in high regard. The word appears 56 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it is used broadly rather than for one rare idea. Its exact force—whether describing a person, reputation, possession, or condition—depends on the sentence in which it appears.

This verb means “destroy utterly”: to wipe something out completely rather than merely damage or weaken it. It expresses a decisive act of destruction, and its verbal nature points to an action or process rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 10:6. The reference identifies its location, but the precise force in that verse should be understood from the surrounding passage. The word’s central idea remains complete destruction.

gl: marry as next of kin; intermarry
d: marry as next of kin; intermarry

e.t: This verb means to marry as next of kin or to intermarry. It describes marriage that joins people or families who are already related or connected by kinship. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, the word occurs nine times, showing a specific action rather than a general word for every kind of marriage. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea is entering marriage within a family or kinship relationship.

This verb means to forget: to fail to remember something or to let it pass from the mind. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used for forgetting people, past experiences, commands, or important matters. Its 119 occurrences show that it is a normal word for the loss or neglect of remembrance, whether through time, inattention, or deliberate disregard. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “point of the shoulder,” referring to the shoulder area or its distinct point. It is a specific bodily or garment-related location rather than a general word for the whole body. The word occurs 30 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, appearing especially often in Exodus, with further occurrences in Leviticus, Ezekiel, and Sirach. Its recorded range begins at Exodus 25:7 and extends to Sirach 45:8, showing continued use for this particular shoulder location.

This noun describes irritation or rebelliousness—the condition of being stirred into resistance rather than quiet cooperation. It names a resistant attitude, not merely a passing inconvenience. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, so its precise force in Deuteronomy 31:27 depends on that verse’s surrounding text rather than on repeated uses elsewhere. Its central meaning remains irritation expressed through rebellious resistance.

This LXX Greek verb means “eat” or “consume.” It describes taking food or another thing in as an act of consumption. The word is a common action term, appearing 508 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus. Its broad use includes ordinary eating as well as references connected with offerings, food regulations, and daily provision, while the surrounding verse determines the specific object and force.

“Opportunely” means in a timely or suitably chosen way—at a moment when something can be done effectively. It is an adverb, so it describes how an action happens rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, in Sirach 18:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is acting at an appropriate time or taking advantage of a fitting opportunity.

This Greek LXX noun means “beauty,” referring to attractive or pleasing loveliness. It describes something viewed as graceful, splendid, or desirable rather than naming an action. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, including uses in 2 Samuel, Job, Psalms, and other writings. Its precise emphasis—whether outward appearance or a broader quality of pleasantness—depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

This adjective means “significant”: it describes something marked out as meaningful or important rather than ordinary or unnoticed. As an adjective, it gives this quality to a person, thing, statement, or event named in the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 80:4. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is described as significant there; the word itself supplies the basic idea of importance or marked meaning.

Zakchaios, also rendered Zakkheos, is a personal name—a proper noun identifying one individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 10:19. Without the verse text, its specific role in that passage cannot be described further, but the word itself functions simply as the person’s name. It should therefore be understood as a name, not as a general title or abstract concept.

Thelarēsa, also rendered Thelarisa, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once, in Ezra 2:59, and functions as a name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The available wording gives the name’s forms but does not provide a separate everyday definition or explain its origin. Its precise reference in Ezra depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Themmōn is a proper name, rendered “Themmon.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 21:32. The available wording establishes the name itself, while the surrounding verse would be needed to determine exactly what or whom the name identifies there. This is a Greek LXX name and should be kept distinct from similarly rendered names in other biblical language traditions.

Iebousi, also rendered Ievusi, is a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. It identifies a named person, people group, or place only as determined by the surrounding passage; the word itself functions as a name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Judges 19:11 and Ezra 9:1. Without the verse wording and context, its specific referent cannot be stated more precisely.

This LXX noun means “track” or “footstep”—a mark left by someone or something moving, or the steps themselves. It can therefore refer either to a trace that can be followed or to a person’s path as they walk. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, including places where tracks or footsteps are recognized, followed, or described. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

Iōcha; Iokha is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not an ordinary word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship, so its meaning is chiefly the individual it names. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 8:16. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, the available information identifies the name and its location but does not establish further details about the person.

This adverb means “it is good; commendably,” describing an action, statement, or condition as good, proper, or commendable. It tells how something is done or how it ought to be regarded, rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 30 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its use is broader than one isolated setting. The surrounding words determine whether it expresses approval, proper conduct, or a favorable assessment in a particular verse.

This noun means “reconciliation”: the restoring of peace or agreement between parties that have been divided or at odds. It names the condition or result of being brought back into harmony, rather than the action of reconciling itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice—once in Isaiah and once in 2 Maccabees—showing that it can describe restored peace in more than one setting. The surrounding verse determines the specific parties and circumstances involved.

This Greek LXX noun means “tail,” referring to the rear or extending end of an animal or other thing. It is a concrete word rather than a description of character or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all within three verses, so it is relatively uncommon. Its exact reference may be literal or part of an image, but the basic meaning remains the same: the tail or trailing end. The word appears in Exodus, Judges, and Proverbs.

This word refers to a “connexion by marriage” or an “alliance” between families. As a noun, it describes the relationship created when people or households become connected through marriage, rather than referring simply to the wedding ceremony itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and historical setting.

“Lighten” is a verb describing the act of making something less heavy or burdensome. It expresses reducing a load or easing what someone must carry. Within the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs 10 times in 10 verses, showing that it is used across several books but is not especially frequent. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “leave” or “remain.” It describes either departing from a place or person, or continuing to be present when others or something else has gone. The precise sense depends on the sentence in which it appears. It occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including uses in Job, Proverbs, Wisdom, Sirach, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its central idea is what is left behind or what continues in place.

This noun means “lobe of the ear,” referring to the soft lower part of the ear. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in Exodus 29:20 and Leviticus 8:24. Both references belong to instructions concerning the ear, and the word identifies the specific part touched or involved rather than the ear generally. Its meaning is therefore concrete and anatomical, naming a distinct portion of the human ear.

Massam is a proper name, referring to a person named Massam rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Genesis 25:13. The available wording preserves the name as “Massam,” so its ordinary meaning is its function as a personal designation. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s place in that passage, but the word itself identifies an individual by name.

Meera, also rendered Mira, is a proper name identifying a person rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 27:13. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide an additional descriptive definition or explanation of its meaning. Its precise significance in that passage belongs to the surrounding verse and context.

Melchiram is a proper name referring to a person named in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal designation rather than a general description, action, or quality. The name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 3:18. Without the surrounding verse text, no further statement about this individual or the significance of the name should be added. The form is also rendered as “Melkhiram,” preserving the name rather than translating it as an ordinary word.

This Greek LXX verb means “reverse”: to turn something back or cause a direction, condition, or course to change. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its exact sense depends on what is being turned or changed in the sentence. The word occurs 31 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Isaiah, Job, and 4 Maccabees. Its central idea remains a reversal or turning back from one state or direction to another.

Nabal is a proper name referring to a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered as “Nabal” and appears 21 times across 19 verses, from 1 Samuel 25 through 2 Samuel 3. Because this is a personal name rather than a common noun or descriptive term, its basic meaning is identification: it names the individual called Nabal. The name also appears as “Naval” in the lexical definition, but the supplied references consistently render it “Nabal.”

“By night” means during nighttime, identifying when an action or event takes place. It is an adverb, so it describes the time associated with something happening rather than naming a person, place, or object. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times, all in deuterocanonical books. Its basic meaning is straightforward: something happens during the night. The surrounding verse determines what action or event is being placed at that time.

“Noemin” is a proper name—the Greek LXX form used to identify a person named Noemin. It functions as a personal name rather than a description, action, or general concept. The name appears 23 times across 22 verses, all within Ruth, from Ruth 1:2 through Ruth 4:17. Its repeated use marks the same named person throughout that book, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain her specific role in any particular passage.

Odouias is a personal name, also rendered “Othoias.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 27:9. The available information identifies the name and its single occurrence, but the verse text is not provided here, so the person’s specific role must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

This verb means “assist”: to provide help or support to someone. As an action word, it describes coming to another person’s aid rather than merely identifying a person or thing. In the LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 30:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of helping or assisting. The word belongs to the Greek LXX corpus and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament occurrence.

Oulamlous, also rendered Ulamlus, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or relationship. It identifies a named individual or place in the Greek Old Testament, but the available information does not establish which one. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Genesis 28:19. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from the surrounding verse and passage, not from the name alone.

Uri is a personal name, also rendered Ouri. It identifies people in the Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs six times across five verses, appearing in 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles. Because it is a proper name, its meaning in any particular passage comes from the person being identified there, not from a separate definition of the name itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “heat to excess”: to make something excessively hot or overheated. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Deuteronomy 19:6. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included, its specific force in that passage cannot be described further; however, its basic meaning remains the act of heating beyond what is ordinary or appropriate.

This verb means “accompany” or “follow.” It describes going along with someone or coming after them, whether by physical movement or by continuing in the same course. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears twice, both in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains movement with or behind another person. It is a verb describing an action, not a person or object.

This noun means a “small light shield,” referring to a protective weapon used in battle. It describes a shield that could be carried and used by fighting forces, rather than a large defensive barrier. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in Ezekiel, where it is associated with armed groups and their equipment. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “of rock” or “rocky,” describing something made of, connected with, or characterized by rock. It is used in the Greek Old Testament’s LXX text, where it occurs four times, all in Joshua. Its basic function is descriptive: it identifies a material or quality associated with rock rather than naming a person, place, or action. The surrounding wording determines exactly what rocky or rock-related thing is being described in each occurrence.

This adjective means “various” or “varied,” describing things that differ from one another rather than being all alike. It can qualify a group, appearance, kind, or set of features, depending on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 25 times across 24 verses, with uses ranging from Genesis through 4 Maccabees. Its central idea remains diversity or difference within what is being described.

This Greek LXX word describes something drunk or suitable for drinking. As an adjective or noun, it can refer either to the condition of being intoxicated or to something intended as a drink. Its basic meaning is stated as “drunk; fit for drinking.” It occurs eight times in seven Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX, including passages in Judges, 1 Samuel, Esther, Job, and Proverbs. The surrounding verse determines which aspect is intended.

This adjective means “ancestral”: it describes something connected with a person’s ancestors or forefathers. It identifies a family, inheritance, tradition, or other matter as belonging to an earlier generation rather than to the present alone. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the noun it describes and the surrounding sentence.

This noun describes a person’s “predisposition” or “eagerness”—an inclination or readiness to act willingly. It names an attitude of readiness rather than an action itself, so its precise force in the single occurrence depends on the surrounding wording. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) corpus, in Sirach 45:23. Though it is narrowly attested, its basic meaning is clear: a ready inclination toward what is to be done.

This Greek LXX verb means “summon”: to call someone to come or appear. It describes an intentional call directed toward a person, rather than a casual mention or general announcement. The word occurs 24 times across the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, showing repeated use for calling people together or bringing someone before another person. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on who is calling and whom they summon.

This word means “mask,” referring to a covering worn over the face. It is a noun, so it names the object itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 15:15. The word’s basic meaning is clear, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how the mask functions in that passage.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “clap the wings,” describing the movement of wings as they strike or flutter together. It is an action word rather than a name for the wings themselves. The word occurs twice in the Greek text, both times in Ezekiel, at Ezekiel 1:23 and 3:13. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the motion of wings being clapped or flapped.

This Greek Old Testament noun means a rent or chink—a narrow opening, crack, or split in something. It describes a physical gap rather than an action or personal quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Isaiah 7:19, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains a break or opening through which something may pass. This is a distinct Greek LXX word and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament occurrence.

Sali is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 2 Chronicles 20:31. Because the name is preserved as a personal designation and no additional definition or verse text is provided here, its meaning is simply the identification of that person. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a proper name.

Sebani, also rendered Sevani, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament, specifically in the book of Nehemiah. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Nehemiah 10:5. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes identity but does not explain the person’s role or significance in that passage.

This adverb means “hardly,” indicating that an action or condition is only barely the case. It qualifies a statement or verb by limiting it, rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, each in a different verse, so its basic sense remains consistent while the surrounding sentence determines exactly what is being limited. References span Genesis, 1 Samuel, and Isaiah.

This LXX word means “barren,” describing a condition in which a woman does not bear children. It is a plain descriptive term for childlessness or inability to conceive, depending on the sentence where it appears. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, and Judges. Its exact force in any verse comes from the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX verb means “take hold of” or “conceive.” It may describe physically grasping someone or something, or becoming pregnant, with the surrounding sentence determining which sense is intended. The word appears 107 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is used in more than one setting while retaining this central idea of taking hold—whether by grasping or by conception. It occurs from Genesis through Song of Songs in the LXX corpus.

Syra, also rendered Sira, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Genesis, 1 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. Because it is a personal name, its specific reference must be determined from the surrounding passage in each occurrence; the name itself supplies identification rather than a broader concept or definition.

This adjective describes something that brings a matter to its completion or end. It points to an action, process, or result that reaches its intended finish, rather than remaining incomplete. The word appears once in the Greek LXX, in Deuteronomy 23:18, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: bringing something to an end.

This word means “working wonders.” It functions as an adjective or noun, describing someone or something connected with wondrous works. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once each in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its precise role in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the performance or characterization of wondrous activity.

This word means “knife”: a noun for a cutting instrument. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 30:14. Its basic meaning identifies the object itself rather than an action, person, or quality. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s exact force in that occurrence must be understood from its sentence and context. The lexical sense remains straightforward: it refers to a knife.

Tophol, also written Tofol, is a proper name preserved as the name of a specific biblical entity. It is not a general description or action word, so its meaning is primarily identification rather than a quality or activity. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Deuteronomy 1:1. The available rendering gives it as “Tophol,” while the lexical definition also records “Tofol.” The surrounding verse text is needed to explain what this named entity represents in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “spread under”: to place or extend something beneath another thing. It describes an action rather than an object, so its basic sense is laying something underneath as a covering, support, or surface. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Isaiah, Ezekiel, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on what is being placed beneath and what it supports or covers.

Perasim is a name preserved as “Perasim” in the Greek Old Testament text. It does not function as an ordinary descriptive word meaning an action, quality, or object; it identifies a named entity. This LXX form occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 14:11, so its normal meaning is limited to that name rather than a broader vocabulary concept. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain what Perasim refers to there.

Phthaiel is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or common object. The name is also rendered “Phthaiēl” and “Fthil.” In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Joshua 19:27. Because it is a personal name, its lexical function is identification: it names an individual, while the surrounding passage supplies the details about that person. The name itself does not provide a broader definition or describe a general concept.

This Greek noun means “heat” or “passion,” describing an intense inner force or ardor. It can refer to strong feeling rather than ordinary warmth, so the surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is emotional intensity or burning heat. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 3:17. The word’s central idea is powerful intensity—something stirred or burning within a person. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This proper name refers to the people called “Phylistiim” or “Filistim” in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal name for a distinct people, rather than as a description of an action or quality. The word occurs 23 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, beginning in Genesis and continuing through 1 Maccabees. Its appearances include references in Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, Judges, and Sirach.

This noun means “papyrus roll,” referring to a rolled writing document made from papyrus. It names a physical object rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, all within the book of Jeremiah, and its use extends across 11 verses. The word’s basic sense remains focused and concrete: a written roll or scroll made of papyrus. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.h: Grow Rank or Run to Grass
e.t: This verb means “run to grass” or “grow rank,” describing vegetation becoming abundant and overgrown. It refers to grass or plant growth rather than a person’s action or character. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Proverbs 24:31. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is the flourishing or uncontrolled growth of grass and weeds.

This verb means to falter in speech or speak inarticulately. It describes speech that does not come out clearly or fluently, so the speaker struggles to express words plainly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Isaiah. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains difficulty or lack of clarity in speaking. The word is found in Isaiah 29:24 and Isaiah 32:4.
